title: Google Dismantles XCPE Botnet Hidden in 1.3 Million Android TV Boxes
excerpt: Google says Videostrong, an Android device maker, intentionally preloaded a firmware backdoor that turned its set-top boxes into a proxy and ad-fraud botnet, and it has banned the company from certified Android devices after a coordinated takedown.
body:
• Google and partners dismantled the XCPE botnet last week, which had enrolled more than 1.3 million set-top boxes, and Google assesses with high confidence that device maker Videostrong intentionally built the backdoor for financial gain.
  • The backdoor, called x.cpe, was preloaded in firmware with system privileges, disabled Google Play Protect, and let operators install apps silently, run shell commands, capture screens and route traffic through owners' home connections.
  • Google took legal action against the control servers for Videostrong and for more than a dozen affiliate malware families, action it assesses will sever access to at least 10 million more compromised devices, and banned Videostrong from certified Android devices.
  • For readers with a low-cost or MECOOL-branded Android TV box: the takedown cut off the servers but did not remove the code from boxes, which reinstalls on reboot, so coverage of the takedown says owners need clean firmware or should disconnect a suspect box from the internet.

Google and industry partners have dismantled a botnet built into the firmware of more than 1.3 million Android set-top boxes, and Google says the manufacturer put it there deliberately. In its report, "Shutting the Door on the XCPE Botnet," published on November 2, the Google Threat Intelligence Group said it assesses with high confidence that the backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed and operated for financial gain by Videostrong Technology Co., an Android original equipment manufacturer and original design manufacturer that builds devices under its own brands and for other labels.

Videostrong monetized the backdoor by selling access to criminal affiliates and loading their malware modules onto devices, Google said. Those modules conducted ad fraud, silently enrolled devices into residential proxy networks, and loaded more malware. Google said the campaign was not a rogue insider or an oversight.

How the backdoor worked

The backdoor operates at system privilege level as x.cpe, running as com.oemservice in some builds, preloaded in the firmware partition, Google said. If uninstalled, it reinstalls from the /oem/ partition on reboot. Since at least late 2024, it had evolved into a modular, three-stage system built to serve multiple paying affiliates at once.

Through a persistent MQTT connection to a command server, operators could silently install applications, execute shell commands, capture the screen, inject keystrokes and carry out network reconnaissance, Google said. The backdoor also disables Google Play Protect. Google said Videostrong used obfuscation to exploit a gap in its compatibility tests and load the code only after a device's first boot, so it was not present when certification checks ran.

Most infected devices were Android TV set-top boxes, Google said, but it also observed telehealth devices, karaoke machines and digital signage devices. Partner firm TrendAI counted 1,472,554 infected devices across 206 models between June 3 and October 1, according to coverage of the takedown by Skimwire citing The Hacker News. Most were in Malaysia, Brazil, Iraq, Mexico and Taiwan, but the United States, Germany, the United Kingdom, Australia and Canada each had tens of thousands, that coverage reported. Many were MECOOL-branded boxes, which partner Synthient linked to Videostrong after finding the backdoor preinstalled on a MECOOL KM9PRO Max.

What Google did

Google worked with Japan's National Police Agency, Lumen, HUMAN Security, Plume, Synthient and TrendAI on the disruption last week. It took legal action against the domains and servers Videostrong used to control the botnet, and against the control domains of more than a dozen malware families loaded through the backdoor. Because those affiliates also distribute modules through other channels, Google assesses the second action will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices. That figure is Google's assessment, not an independently verified count.

Google has cut ties with Videostrong and banned it and any future subsidiaries or affiliates from building and selling certified Android devices, supplying software to other certified vendors, or making devices with preloaded Google apps. It said it has improved its firmware-integrity checks for certified Android TV devices.

What owners should do

The takedown removed the control servers, not the code on the boxes, which reinstalls on reboot. Skimwire, citing BleepingComputer, reported that owners would need clean firmware or should disconnect a suspect box from the internet, and advised checking whether a low-cost or MECOOL-branded box's maker is on Google's certified partner list, and changing passwords for accounts signed into on a suspect box from a different device. A model name alone does not prove a box is infected, that coverage noted, citing Synthient's list of 182 model names seen in the campaign.

For households in the United States, the practical check is the box itself: an uncertified, low-cost Android TV box bought for international channels is exactly the class of device this botnet used.
